title: Introduction to Databases
summary: Covers fundamental concepts of databases, DBMS, data models, ANSI/SPARC 3-level architecture, data independence, schemas vs instances, and advantages of DBMS over file-based systems.

definitions.definition: A logically organized collection of related data with some inherent meaning, designed for a specific purpose.
definitions.example: A university database storing student records, courses, and enrollments.

definitions.definition: A general-purpose software system that facilitates defining, constructing, manipulating, and sharing databases among users and applications.
definitions.example: MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL are examples of DBMS software.

definitions.definition: The part of the real world about which data is stored in the database.
definitions.example: For a bank database, the miniworld includes customers, accounts, and transactions.

definitions.definition: The overall design/description of the database structure. It rarely changes once defined.
definitions.example: STUDENT(ID, Name, GPA) describes the structure of the Student table.

definitions.definition: The actual data stored in the database at a particular moment in time. Changes frequently.
definitions.example: The set of all student records currently in the STUDENT table.

definitions.definition: The ability to change the schema at one level without affecting the schema at the next higher level.
definitions.example: Changing how data is stored on disk (physical) without changing the logical schema.

definitions.definition: A 3-level architecture consisting of External (user views), Conceptual (logical structure), and Internal (physical storage) levels.
definitions.example: External: student view showing only grades. Conceptual: full student table. Internal: index files on disk.

definitions.definition: Data about the structure of the database, stored in the DBMS catalog. This is the self-describing nature of a database.
definitions.example: Table names, column types, constraints stored in system tables.

definitions.definition: Hiding storage details and presenting users with a conceptual view of the database.
definitions.example: Users write SQL queries without knowing how data is physically stored.

mustKnowConcepts.title: 3-Level Architecture
mustKnowConcepts.description: External level (user views), Conceptual level (global logical design, describes structure and constraints), Internal level (physical storage). Each level has its own schema.

mustKnowConcepts.title: DBMS vs File Systems
mustKnowConcepts.description: DBMS provides: data abstraction, reduced redundancy, data sharing, integrity, security, concurrency control, backup/recovery. File systems suffer from data redundancy, inconsistency, isolation, and no concurrency control.

mustKnowConcepts.title: Data Independence
mustKnowConcepts.description: Logical independence: change conceptual schema without changing external. Physical independence: change internal schema without changing conceptual.

mustKnowConcepts.title: DBA Responsibilities
mustKnowConcepts.description: Database Administrator authorizes access, monitors usage, acquires resources, handles security and recovery. They are responsible for giving access and monitoring database use.

mustKnowConcepts.title: Types of Database Users
mustKnowConcepts.description: Casual end users (occasional queries), Parametric/naive users (standard queries), Sophisticated users (engineers/analysts who learn DBMS), Stand-alone users.

mustKnowConcepts.title: Database Types
mustKnowConcepts.description: Operational, Distributed (data split across sites), Cloud (remotely maintained via web), Parallel (multiple CPUs), Spatial, Real-time, Multimedia, NoSQL (graph databases use nodes/edges).

examTricks.trick: Conceptual level 'unifies various external views' — don't confuse with physical level
examTricks.explanation: The conceptual/logical level describes the global structure. External = user views. Internal/Physical = storage.

examTricks.trick: Graph database is NoSQL, not SQL
examTricks.explanation: Graph databases (using nodes, edges, properties) fall under NoSQL category, not traditional SQL.

examTricks.trick: Cloud database key distinction: can reside remotely, maintained through web browsers
examTricks.explanation: This is the defining feature that distinguishes cloud databases from other types.

examTricks.trick: Parallel databases improve processing using multiple CPUs
examTricks.explanation: Don't confuse with distributed databases which spread data across geographic locations.

examTricks.trick: Self-describing nature is stored in DBMS catalog, not application program
examTricks.explanation: The metadata/catalog stores the database description — this is what makes it self-describing.

confusedConcepts.difference: Schema is the structure/design (rarely changes). Instance is the actual data at a point in time (changes frequently).
confusedConcepts.howToRemember: Schema = blueprint of a house. Instance = the furniture inside at any given moment.

confusedConcepts.difference: Conceptual is the single global logical design. External is individual user views (there can be many).
confusedConcepts.howToRemember: Conceptual = the whole building plan. External = each apartment's floor plan.

confusedConcepts.difference: Distributed: data across geographic sites on a network. Parallel: multiple CPUs in same location for speed.
confusedConcepts.howToRemember: Distributed = offices in different cities. Parallel = multiple workers in same office.

keyPoints: Each level has its own schema
NOT: data analysis and statistics (exam trick!)
Domain = set of permitted values for an attribute

title: ER Modeling
summary: Covers Entity-Relationship (ER) diagrams including entities, attributes, relationships, cardinality ratios, participation constraints, weak entities, and keys.

definitions.definition: Any object in the system that we want to model and store information about.
definitions.example: STUDENT, COURSE, EMPLOYEE are entities.

definitions.definition: A property that describes an entity. Can be simple, composite, multi-valued, or derived.
definitions.example: Name (composite: FirstName + LastName), Age (derived from DateOfBirth), Phone (multi-valued).

definitions.definition: An attribute that uniquely identifies individual entities of an entity type.
definitions.example: StudentID uniquely identifies each student.

definitions.definition: An entity that cannot be uniquely identified by its own attributes alone. It depends on an owning/identifying entity for its existence.
definitions.example: SECTION depends on COURSE. SECTION's key = (CourseID + SectionNo).

definitions.definition: An association between two or more entities.
definitions.example: WORKS_FOR relationship between EMPLOYEE and DEPARTMENT.

definitions.definition: Specifies the maximum number of relationship instances an entity can participate in. Types: 1:1, 1:M, M:N.
definitions.example: Each department has ONE manager (1:1). Each department has MANY employees (1:M). Students take MANY courses and courses have MANY students (M:N).

definitions.definition: Total (every entity must participate, double line) vs Partial (some entities may not participate, single line).
definitions.example: Every employee MUST work for a department (total). Not every employee manages a department (partial).

definitions.definition: An attribute that can be divided into smaller sub-parts.
definitions.example: Address → (Street, City, State, Zip)

definitions.definition: An attribute whose value can be calculated from other attributes.
definitions.example: AGE derived from DATE_OF_BIRTH.

mustKnowConcepts.title: ER Diagram Symbols
mustKnowConcepts.description: Rectangle = Entity, Ellipse = Attribute, Diamond = Relationship, Double rectangle = Weak entity, Double ellipse = Multi-valued attribute, Dashed ellipse = Derived attribute.

mustKnowConcepts.title: Cardinality Ratios
mustKnowConcepts.description: 1:1 (one-to-one), 1:M (one-to-many), M:N (many-to-many). Students-Courses is M:N. Department-Manager is 1:1.

mustKnowConcepts.title: Weak Entity Identification
mustKnowConcepts.description: Weak entity has no key of its own. Uses partial key + owner's key. Connected via identifying relationship (double diamond). Always has total participation.

mustKnowConcepts.title: Participation: Total vs Partial
mustKnowConcepts.description: Total = double line (must participate). Partial = single line (may participate). Total means existence dependency.

mustKnowConcepts.title: Attribute Types
mustKnowConcepts.description: Simple (atomic), Composite (divisible), Multi-valued (multiple values), Derived (calculated), Key (unique identifier).

examTricks.trick: Weak entity key = partial key + owner's primary key combined
examTricks.explanation: SECTION key is (CourseID, SectionNo), not just SectionNo alone.

examTricks.trick: Derived attribute represented by dashed ellipse
examTricks.explanation: AGE calculated from DATE_OF_BIRTH is derived — shown with dashed outline.
One student takes many courses AND one course has many students = M:N.
Common mistake: confusing shapes. Rectangle=Entity, Diamond=Relationship, Ellipse=Attribute.

examTricks.trick: An entity's attribute can be simple, composite, or multi-valued — it CAN be composite (exam: 'all of these')
examTricks.explanation: When asked 'what is true about entity attributes', answer is often 'all of the above' including simple, composite, and multi-valued.

confusedConcepts.difference: Strong has its own key attribute. Weak depends on another entity (owner) and uses partial key.
confusedConcepts.howToRemember: Strong = independent adult. Weak = child depending on parent for identity.

confusedConcepts.difference: Total (double line): ALL entities must participate. Partial (single line): SOME entities may not participate.
confusedConcepts.howToRemember: Total = mandatory attendance. Partial = optional attendance.

confusedConcepts.difference: Composite: can be split into parts (Name → First+Last). Multi-valued: can have multiple values (Phone numbers).
confusedConcepts.howToRemember: Composite = splitting a pizza into slices. Multi-valued = having multiple pizzas.

keyPoints: Super key: any set that uniquely identifies
Foreign key: references another table's PK

title: Enhanced ER & ER-to-Relational Mapping
summary: Covers Enhanced ER concepts (specialization, generalization, superclass/subclass, union types) and rules for mapping ER diagrams to relational schemas.

definitions.definition: Top-down process of defining subclasses of an entity type by identifying distinguishing characteristics.
definitions.example: EMPLOYEE specialized into SECRETARY, ENGINEER, TECHNICIAN.

definitions.definition: Bottom-up process of identifying common characteristics among entity types and creating a generalized superclass.
definitions.example: CAR and TRUCK generalized into VEHICLE.

definitions.definition: Superclass is the parent entity. Subclass inherits all attributes of the superclass and may have additional specific attributes.
definitions.example: PERSON (superclass) → EMPLOYEE, STUDENT (subclasses).

definitions.definition: An entity can be a member of at most ONE subclass. Marked with 'd' in the circle.
definitions.example: A person is either MALE or FEMALE, not both.

definitions.definition: An entity can be a member of MORE THAN ONE subclass. Marked with 'o' in the circle.
definitions.example: An employee can be both a MANAGER and an ENGINEER.

definitions.definition: Every entity in the superclass MUST belong to at least one subclass. Double line to circle.
definitions.example: Every PERSON must be either STUDENT or EMPLOYEE.

definitions.definition: An entity in the superclass may NOT belong to any subclass. Single line to circle.
definitions.example: Not every EMPLOYEE needs to be a MANAGER.

definitions.definition: A subclass that has multiple parent entity types (multiple superclasses). Differs from specialization which has one parent.
definitions.example: OWNER can be a PERSON or a COMPANY (two different parent types).

definitions.definition: Each subclass has only one parent superclass. Forms a tree structure.
definitions.example: EMPLOYEE → ENGINEER → SENIOR_ENGINEER (single-parent chain).

definitions.definition: A subclass can have multiple superclasses. Differs from hierarchy.
definitions.example: STUDENT_EMPLOYEE inherits from both STUDENT and EMPLOYEE.

mustKnowConcepts.title: ER-to-Relational Mapping Rules
mustKnowConcepts.description: Step 1: Map regular entities → tables. Step 2: Map weak entities (include owner's PK). Step 3: Map 1:1 relationships (FK on either side, prefer total participation side). Step 4: Map 1:M (FK on M-side). Step 5: Map M:N (create new junction table). Step 6: Map multi-valued attributes (separate table).

mustKnowConcepts.title: M:N Mapping Creates Additional Relation
mustKnowConcepts.description: Many-to-many relationships generate an additional/new relation (junction table) containing FKs from both entities.

mustKnowConcepts.title: Disjoint (d) vs Overlapping (o)
mustKnowConcepts.description: 'd' in circle: member of at most ONE subclass. 'o' in circle: can be member of MULTIPLE subclasses.

mustKnowConcepts.title: Total vs Partial Specialization
mustKnowConcepts.description: Total (double line): every superclass entity MUST be in some subclass. Partial (single line): some may not be in any subclass.

mustKnowConcepts.title: Recursive Relationship Mapping
mustKnowConcepts.description: A relationship from entity to itself. Mapped by adding a FK in the same table referencing its own PK.

mustKnowConcepts.title: Counting Relations from ERD
mustKnowConcepts.description: 1:1 → usually 1-2 relations. 1:M → 2 relations (FK on M-side). M:N → 3 relations (extra junction table). Weak entity → included with owner's PK.

examTricks.trick: M:N mapping always generates an ADDITIONAL relation — answer is never 'merge' or 'ignore'
examTricks.explanation: This is tested almost every year. M:N → new table with both PKs as composite key.

examTricks.trick: Recursive relationship = FK referencing own table's PK
examTricks.explanation: Example: EMPLOYEE supervises EMPLOYEE. Add Supervisor_SSN FK in EMPLOYEE table.

examTricks.trick: Counting relations from ERD: count entities + extra tables for M:N relationships
examTricks.explanation: Two entities with 1:1 = 1 or 2 tables. Two entities with M:N = 3 tables.

examTricks.trick: Leaf node in specialization hierarchy has no subclasses
examTricks.explanation: A leaf node is the bottom-most subclass — it has no further specializations.

examTricks.trick: Lattice vs Hierarchy: lattice allows multiple superclasses
examTricks.explanation: Hierarchy = one parent per subclass (tree). Lattice = multiple parents allowed (graph).

confusedConcepts.difference: Specialization is top-down (dividing entity into subgroups). Generalization is bottom-up (combining entities into superclass).
confusedConcepts.howToRemember: Specialization = zooming IN. Generalization = zooming OUT.

confusedConcepts.difference: Union type has MULTIPLE parent entities. Specialization has ONE parent entity.
confusedConcepts.howToRemember: Union = child with two different families. Specialization = siblings in same family.

confusedConcepts.difference: Hierarchy: each subclass has exactly one parent (tree). Lattice: a subclass can have multiple parents.
confusedConcepts.howToRemember: Hierarchy = family tree. Lattice = complex web of relationships.

keyPoints: 1:1 → FK on either side (prefer total participation)
M:N → New junction table with both PKs
Weak entity → Include owner's PK in its table
Total = must belong to a subclass (double line)
(m) = member of one or more subclasses (overlapping concept)
